analysis.one_liner: Extends children's online privacy law to teens, banning targeted ads and giving families deletion rights.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan privacy bill for kids and teens, with 22 Senate cosponsors, cleared the Senate Commerce Committee and was placed on the Senate calendar, but never received a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would update a 1998 law that protects kids' online data so it also covers teenagers 13 to 16. Websites and apps could no longer collect or use a child's or teen's personal information to target ads at them, would have to collect only the data they need, delete it when a family asks, keep it secure, and tell users if data is sent abroad. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the rules. The bill cleared its committee with a substitute amendment that dropped several of the original bill's provisions and was placed on the Senate calendar, but the full Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Children under 13 and teens 13 to 16 who use websites, apps, games, and connected devices, along with their parents, who gain new rights to see, delete, and correct the data companies hold about their kids.

how_it_helps.text: The bill extends the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act to 'teens' — individuals over 12 and under 17 — so its notice, consent, and deletion rules cover teenagers for the first time [S2].

It makes it unlawful for an operator to collect, use, disclose, or compile a child's or teen's personal information for individual-specific advertising — ads aimed at a particular person based on their data, psychological profiling, or device identifiers [S2].

Parents of children and teens themselves can request a description of the data collected, delete it at any time, refuse further collection, and challenge inaccurate information, and companies cannot cut off service because a family made a deletion request [S2].

It restricts collection to information reasonably necessary for the service the child or teen requested, limits how long data can be kept, requires disclosure when personal information is stored or transferred outside the United States, and requires reasonable security practices [S2].
The FTC could seek civil penalties above its usual statutory caps to deter violations, and state attorneys general could sue on behalf of their residents [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Online platforms, app makers, and the advertising-technology companies whose business depends on collecting personal data and serving targeted ads, which would lose ad revenue and bear compliance costs. The bill keeps a 'safe harbor' system letting companies follow FTC-approved self-regulatory guidelines written by industry representatives in place of some regulatory requirements.

drawbacks.text: The committee substitute that was reported stripped major pieces of the original bill, including the standalone 'Digital Marketing Bill of Rights for Teens,' a broader targeted-marketing ban section, and the planned Youth Privacy and Marketing Division inside the FTC, leaving a narrower bill [S2].

The reported bill retains FTC-approved 'safe harbor' guidelines issued by representatives of the marketing or online industries, with companies deemed compliant if they follow them, and requires FTC incentives for self-regulation [S2].
Key protections depend on future FTC rulemaking and take effect 180 days after rules or enactment, so families would not get immediate protection [S2].
The bill exempts nonprofits from coverage and carves out children's voice audio files from the definition of personal information if they are used only to perform a task and deleted immediately [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to children and parents are real: teens would get privacy rights they currently lack entirely under the 1998 law, and behavioral ad targeting at minors would be barred. The costs fall on data-driven advertising companies, which is the point of the bill. The honest caveats are that the version reported by the committee was significantly narrower than the original, key rules depend on future FTC rulemaking, and the industry-written safe harbor system softens enforcement. None of these caveats change who wins and loses; they change how strong the protection would have been.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee reported the bill favorably and placed it on the Senate calendar in December 2023, but no floor vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey introduced the bill on May 3, 2023, together with Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Republican, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee [S1] [S2] [S4].
On July 27, 2023, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute [S4].
On December 13, 2023, Senator Cantwell reported the bill with a substitute amendment and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 288 [S2] [S4].

The reported substitute deleted large sections of the original bill text, including the Digital Marketing Bill of Rights for Teens, the targeted-marketing section, and the Youth Privacy and Marketing Division, leaving a narrower set of protections [S2].
The bill never received a vote in the full Senate before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1] [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Internet platforms and advertising-technology companies are better off because the bill died: they continue collecting and monetizing minors' personal data under the 1998 rules, which still cover only children under 13 and leave teens with essentially no federal online privacy rights.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.role: Lead sponsor; author of the original 1998 children's privacy law
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited bipartisan support

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Joined Markey in introducing the bill

for.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
for.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill out of committee with a substitute amendment and placed it on the Senate calendar

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill, which sat on the Senate calendar for over a year, to the floor for a vote

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: a Democratic lead sponsor with a Republican co-introducer and 22 cosponsors split roughly evenly between the parties (8 Republicans, 13 Democrats, 1 independent), and the committee reported it favorably; no recorded opposition vote ever occurred because the bill never reached the floor.

industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful to collect, use, or compile a child's or teen's personal information for individual-specific advertising, removing a core revenue stream built on profiling minors. Its gain would come directly at the expense of the privacy protections the bill gives families.

industries.industry: Internet platforms, app makers, and connected-device companies
industries.note: Platforms would face new collection limits, retention limits, deletion and correction rights, security duties, and disclosure rules for data sent abroad, plus FTC penalties above the usual caps. Industry representatives could soften the impact through FTC-approved self-regulatory 'safe harbor' guidelines that the bill preserves.
The bill restricts disclosing children's and teens' personal information to third parties and limits ad-measurement uses that rely on targeted marketing, shrinking the market for minors' data.
